title: 5 reasons to only lift heavy weight DEBUNKED
summary: NH debunks five justifications for only lifting heavy low-rep weights: that it's less fatiguing, less mentally stressful, that you must lift big to get big, that strength equals size, and that form breakdown doesn't matter. He argues bodybuilders need set multiplication and tonnage across rep ranges, that 1RMs are a powerlifting practice useless for hypertrophy, and mocks the 'nu-powerlifter'.
claims: Only heavy lifting and only volume are both emotional positions, not programming reasoning
By 'only heavy' he means only very high intensity at low reps
A true one rep max is less fatiguing overall than 10 reps; reps at high intensity are always more tiring in global tonnage
Being out of breath after a single deadlift or squat rep means garbage cardio
People who call anything over five reps 'cardio' often lack work capacity, and avoiding reps reinforces that weakness so volume never builds
Doing 1-3 reps on every movement makes volume almost nonexistent; low-rep minimalists barely do accessories or isolation
A 1RM is one second of stress, while an 8-rep squat set is mentally harder; staying in low reps is a comfort zone
Refusing set multiplication means refusing to multiply training volume
Prominent powerlifters now promote reps and the full range of RPEs for strength too
One rep maxes are a powerlifting practice for learning to max or peaking; bodybuilders have no use for them and they are counterproductive for hypertrophy
Bodybuilding is about building strength because it builds tonnage and muscle, not testing it
You can lift heavy at 15, 8 or 5 reps; the more tonnage in relevant intensity windows, the better
One rep maxes don't build strength; 2-3RMs or sets with one rep in the tank might, but 1RMs are a waste of time
You can't tell someone's strength from their size; strength does not equal size
'Strength equals size' is used to justify bulking to very high body fat, which misses the point of bodybuilding
Strength progression that stays in low rep ranges translates to little muscle long-term; someone progressing less but training higher reps will be bigger
Focusing on tonnage within relevant intensity windows will not misguide you
When low reps are your only tool and you stall, you grind ugly reps; form breaks down, shifting tonnage away from target muscles and raising injury risk
Heavy-only lifters cycle through getting hurt, rehabbing with light weights and going heavy again, ending up strong but small
The 'nu-powerlifter' neither competes nor follows powerlifting principles like RPE or accessories, nor trains like a bodybuilder
Intensity is not tied to rep range; you can train at 95% intensity with 10 reps
